cues.en: What we're going to talk about today is CQRS and event sourcing and this is actually a big problem just on the slide. Everyone always talks about CQRS and event sourcing when really it's event sourcing and CQRS. When I first started teaching people about CQRS and event sourcing, it was advantageous to teach them CQRS first and then teach them event sourcing. You can use CQRS without event sourcing, but with event sourcing you must use CQRS.
cues.zh: 我们今天要聊的是 CQRS 和事件溯源，其实光是幻灯片上这个标题就有点问题。大家总把“CQRS 与事件溯源”挂在嘴边，但实际上应该是“事件溯源与 CQRS”。我最初向大家普及这些概念时，先讲 CQRS 再讲事件溯源更易于理解。你可以单独使用 CQRS 而不用事件溯源，但如果用了事件溯源，你就必须使用 CQRS。

cues.en: And we're going to talk about what both of those concepts are. I've been talking about this subject for a very, very long time. In fact, the first time I ever did talk about this was in 2006 at QCon San Francisco. And actually, some of the slides are still the same from all the way back then. I have probably done this or a similar talk 50 times over the last couple of years. When I did the first talk, it was actually awful.
cues.zh: 我们接下来会讲讲这两个概念到底是什么。这个主题我已经讲了非常非常久了。实际上，我第一次讲还是在 2006 年旧金山的 QCon 上。甚至今天的一些幻灯片还是当年那套。在过去的几年里，这个或类似的主题我大概讲过 50 次了。当年第一次讲的时候，现场其实惨不忍睹。

cues.en: So, I come in and I've never really talked at conferences or anything like that before. And I'm talking about domain-driven design and messaging systems and these new patterns. And I come in and my front row is Martin Fowler, Eric Evans, and Gregor Hopay. I'd never met any of them before. I think I went through my entire 60-minute talk in something like 17 seconds. We will not do that today.
cues.zh: 当时我走上台，之前从来没在技术大会这种场合做过演讲。我要讲的是领域驱动设计、消息系统以及这些新模式。结果我一进场，第一排坐着 Martin Fowler、Eric Evans 和 Gregor Hopay。我之前从没见过他们任何一位。我觉得我整整 60 分钟的演讲，大概 17 秒钟就全秃噜完了。今天我们可不会这样了。

cues.en: first started looking at things like event sourcing and where the ideas came from. They're not new ideas. In fact, when I used to work with mainframes before SQL databases got popular,
cues.zh: 最初研究的是事件溯源这类东西，以及这些想法从何而来。它们并不是新概念。为了写这本书、梳理事件溯源的历史，我一路追溯到了美索不达米亚和苏美尔。所以如果之后你来找我说，我怎么说服公司用这些新技术？它们可不新。人们已经做了几十年了。事实上，在 SQL 数据库流行之前，我还在用大型机的时候，

cues.en: This is actually how we tended to build systems. Your database actually works with event sourcing internally. But at the time, I was working with algorithmic trading. And when you're working with algorithmic trading, you really, really need a safety net. You need everything in your system to be deterministic, so you can go back to any point in time and figure out exactly what was going on. Why? Because what happens when you're doing 500 trades per second and your algorithm decides it wants to find places it can lose one penny at a time?
cues.zh: 我们其实就是这样构建系统的。你的数据库内部其实就在用事件溯源。但当时我在做算法交易。做算法交易时，你非常非常需要一张安全网。你需要系统里的一切都是确定性的，这样你才能回到任何一个时间点，弄清楚当时到底发生了什么。为什么？因为当你每秒做 500 笔交易，而你的算法决定要去找那些能一次亏一便士的地方时，会发生什么？

cues.en: you can find a whole lot of places to lose money in the stock market. The other thing that we need is we need to be able to look and do scientific measurements over time. And we need to be able to compare time periods to time periods. We need to do this in a deterministic way. But the biggest thing that we needed was an audit log. How many of you have an audit log today for your system? Raise your hand. Okay, now keep your hand up if you can prove that your audit log is correct. What's the point of your audit log?
cues.zh: 在股市里，你能找到一大堆亏钱的地方。我们需要的另一点是，能够观察并随时间做科学测量。我们需要能够把不同时间段拿来互相比较。我们需要以确定性的方式做到这一点。但我们最需要的是一份审计日志。今天你们有多少人的系统有审计日志？举手。好，现在如果你能证明你的审计日志是正确的，就继续举着。你的审计日志意义何在？

cues.en: if you can't prove that it's correct. I know some characters that had this problem. Hansel and Gretel were walking through the forest and they got lost. So they started leaving an audit log, correct? They started leaving little pieces of bread. So they would know where they were and they'd be able to get back. Unfortunately, the little woodland critters were coming behind them and eating the bread. They couldn't prove their audit log was correct. I would argue they would have been better off in the story if they had not had an audit log at all because, well, they would have...
cues.zh: 如果你没法证明它是正确的。我知道有些角色就遇到过这种麻烦。Hansel 和 Gretel 走在森林里迷路了。于是他们开始留审计日志，对吧？他们一路撒面包屑。这样他们就能知道自己走到了哪，并且能找路回去。不幸的是，林子里的小动物跟在后面把面包全吃了。他们根本没法证明自己的审计日志是正确的。我甚至觉得，在这个故事里，要是他们当初压根不留审计日志反而会更好，因为，呃，他们就能……

cues.en: had the piece of bread when they got to the house. They wouldn't have been hungry. They never would have gone in. They wouldn't have ended up in the oven, which is the real ending of the story if you read the real story. But this is a big problem. We have audit logs that we can't prove are correct. And this is one of the main things we are trying to solve, is we need an audit log that we could prove was actually correct. And there's a lot of industries you need to do this. Anything regulated, you need to be able to prove that your audit log is actually what happened. We're going to go through some cases, real cases, where people
cues.zh: 在到达屋子时吃掉那些面包。他们就不会挨饿，也绝不会走进去，更不会差点被塞进烤箱——如果你读过原版故事，那才是真正的结局。但这是个大问题：我们拥有无法证明其正确性的审计日志。而这正是我们努力解决的核心问题之一：我们需要能够证明其真实正确的审计日志。很多行业都必须做到这一点。在任何受监管的行业，你都得证明审计日志确实反映了真实发生的情况。接下来我们会看几个案例，一些真实的案例，看看人们

cues.en: failed on this and how you can actually solve them. And what we came up with was that every state transition inside of your domain, how many have heard of domain-driven design? So when I say domain, I'm referring to a domain model similar to what's in domain-driven design. An object model, we can imagine, but it may be functional as well. When we talk about a state transition that occurs inside of that model, that should be a first-class concept inside of your system. It's not that update table set
cues.zh: 是如何在这方面栽跟头的，以及你究竟该如何解决。我们得出的结论是，业务领域内的每一次状态转换——有多少人听说过领域驱动设计？所以当我说“领域”时，我指的就是类似于领域驱动设计中的领域模型。我们可以想象成一个对象模型，当然也可以是函数式的。当我们谈论该模型内部发生的状态转换时，它应该成为系统里的一等概念。它绝不是那种 update table set

cues.en: some column equals value, it's a fact. And a fact is what should come out of your domain model. Customer status level promoted. That's very different than update table set column equal. And if you start modeling like this, a lot of your problems will actually go away. What's most interesting for me about event sourcing is that not a single mature industry uses the concept of current state.
cues.zh: 某某字段等于某个值，它是一个事实。而事实才应该是领域模型产生的内容。比如“客户会员等级已晋升”。这跟 update table set column equal 截然不同。如果你开始像这样建模，很多问题其实都会迎刃而解。对我而言，事件溯源最有趣的一点在于：没有任何一个成熟行业在使用“当前状态”这个概念。

cues.en: None. And when I say mature, I do not mean Groupon. I'm thinking finance, banking, insurance. Things that have been around for hundreds of years. Not a single one of them has the concept of current state inside of it. How many of you have a bank account? Do you think your balance is a column in a table? Or is your balance an equation?
cues.zh: 没有。我说成熟，不是指 Groupon。我指的是金融、银行、保险。这些行业已经存在了几百年。它们当中没有一个在内部包含“当前状态”这个概念。你们有多少人有银行账户？你觉得你的余额是表里的一列吗？还是说，你的余额是一个方程式？

cues.en: Your balance is a summation of all the previous transactions value upon your account. What would happen if it were just a column and a table? So you have a disagreement with your bank about what your balance is. You call them up on the phone and say, yes, it says I've got $103, but I think I should have $207. And they go, all hail the mighty column. The column says 103. That's what you have.
cues.zh: 你的余额是你账户上此前所有交易金额的总和。如果它只是表里的一列，会怎样？假设你和银行对余额有分歧。你打电话给他们说，对，上面写我有 103 美元，但我认为我应该是 207 美元。他们却说，膜拜那无所不能的列吧。列说是 103。你就是 103。

cues.en: But today you can call up and we can say, well, I can add up all the things on your account and we can check whether or not it's actually correct. Your balance is a first level derivative off of the facts on your account. And we can do this with all forms of current state. It's not just about things like bank account balances. You can do it to any business problem that you will ever come across. We're talking about this more in a minute, but there's other reasons why they don't keep current state.
cues.zh: 但今天你打电话来，我们可以说，好吧，我可以把你账户上的所有东西加起来，然后检查它到底对不对。你的余额是你账户上各项事实的一阶导数。而且我们可以对所有形式的当前状态都这么做。这不只适用于银行账户余额这类东西。你可以把它用于你遇到的任何业务问题。我们稍后会多谈这一点，但他们不保存当前状态还有其他原因。

cues.en: and instead its current state is transient. It's a first level derivative. This is my quintessential structural model. How many of you have a structural model today? It could be in SQL, it could be in a document database, it could be in an XML file. What it describes is the structure of a piece of data. And this is what we are told to find when we are in university, right? You just gotta find the structure of the data. Structure of data isn't that important.
cues.zh: 相反，它的当前状态是瞬态的。它是一阶导数。这就是我最典型的结构模型。你们有多少人今天有结构模型？它可能在 SQL 里，可能在文档数据库里，可能在 XML 文件里。它描述的是某份数据的结构。而这就是我们在大学时被告知要寻找的东西，对吧？你只要找到数据的结构。数据的结构其实没那么重要。

cues.en: Now let's take this. This is not the only way that I could represent this particular piece of information. I could also represent the same information as a series of events, facts. So now we have cart created, three items added, and shipping information added, which doesn't fit quite right at this resolution. This is actually five events. When I tried to put the three item added, the boxes got really little and you couldn't read them anymore. But I could at any point in time take these five events
cues.zh: 那我们来看看这个。这不是我表示这条特定信息的唯一方式。我也可以把同样的信息表示成一系列事件、事实。现在我们有购物车已创建、添加了三件商品、添加了配送信息，这个分辨率下显示不太合适。这实际上是五个事件。当我试着把“添加三件商品”放进去时，方框变得特别小，已经看不清了。但我可以在任意时刻把这五个事件

cues.en: I could run them through a piece of code, a function, and I could pass you back that, correct? I could take my five events that are saved and transform them to give you back a structural model. And this is what people are doing when they're doing event sourcing. Event sourcing is all about the storing of facts. And any time that you have state structural models, they are first level derivative off of your facts.
cues.zh: 把它们跑过一段代码、一个函数，就能把结果返回给你，对吧？我可以把这五个已保存的事件转换，还原出一个结构化模型给你。这就是人们做事件溯源时在做的事。事件溯源的核心就是存储事实。任何时候你拥有状态化的结构化模型，它们都是事实的一阶派生。

cues.en: and they are transient. When I say transient, it does not mean in memory. Transient means I am willing to delete them. I make them persistent, but I could at any point in time delete them and rebuild it. Could I delete this and then replay those again? Imagine that. Anything in your system you can just delete and replay and get back. There's a lot of differences between these two. How many of you have refactored a domain object before?
cues.zh: 而且它们是瞬态的。我说瞬态，并不是指在内存里。瞬态意味着我愿意把它们删掉。我让它们持久化，但我随时可以删除它们并重建。我能把这个删掉然后重放那些事件吗？想象一下。系统里任何东西你都可以直接删掉、重放、再拿回来。这两者之间有很多差异。你们有多少人重构过领域对象？

cues.en: Renamed something on it. And then you have to go make your SQL migration scripts, correct? What happens when I rename something here? And I'm storing this. When I restart my server, do I need to run a SQL migration script? No. More importantly, what happens when I have two servers that are running side by side? One's running version one, the other one is running version two. Could each server have its own view of what these facts are?
cues.zh: 在上面重命名了某个东西。然后你就得去写 SQL 迁移脚本，对吧？如果我在这里重命名某个东西呢？而我把它存起来。当我重启服务器时，我需要跑 SQL 迁移脚本吗？不需要。更重要的是，当我有两台并排运行的服务器时会发生什么？一台跑版本一，另一台跑版本二。每台服务器能对“这些事实是什么”有各自的视图吗？

cues.en: So one of them has this model, another one has a slightly different model. Sure, there's no problem at all with this. When we start looking at this, our facts come back down to our use cases. And one thing you will learn over time is that structure changes more often than behavior. Your use cases of a system tend to be reasonably stable over long periods of time. How you interpret your internal data, the structure that you use, has a tendency of changing a lot.
cues.zh: 所以其中一台有这个模型，另一台有稍微不同的模型。当然，这完全没问题。当我们开始审视这一点时，我们的事实会回到我们的用例上。随着时间推移你会学到一件事：结构比行为变化得更频繁。一个系统的用例往往在很长一段时间内相当稳定。你如何解读内部数据、你使用的结构，却往往会频繁变化。

cues.en: We haven't gotten to the reason why most businesses that are mature are using this. And this slide I've been using literally since 2006. This slide took me forever to find. And the reason why is you have an accountant erasing something in the middle of their journal. Accountants do not do this unless they work for Enron. You do not erase something in the middle of your ledger. This is highly illegal.
cues.zh: 我们还没讲到为什么大多数成熟的企业都在用这个。这张幻灯片我从 2006 年就一直用到现在。我花了很久才找到这张幻灯片。原因就是：你有个会计在账本中间擦掉某个东西。会计不会这么干，除非他们在给安然干活。你不会在账本中间擦掉东西。这严重违法。

cues.en: If you took in a class in accounting, you were probably told that accountants don't use pencils. They use pens. And it's the same thing we talk about event sourcing. When we talk about event sourcing, you can never, ever update an event. And you can never delete an event. To be fair, there are some circumstances where you want to delete events over long periods of time. And for instance, in our database, we support doing that. Conceptually, you never do it.
cues.zh: 如果你上过会计课，大概会被告知会计不用铅笔，他们用钢笔。我们讲事件溯源时也是一样。讲事件溯源时，事件永远不能更新，也永远不能删除。公平地说，有些情况下你会想在一段很长时间后删除事件。比如，我们的数据库就支持这么做。但在概念上，你永远不这么做。

cues.en: And I know some people in the room are probably going, but that data must get very big over time. How many of you are doing more than 1 million transactions per day? 5 million? 10 million. So I'll give you guys a hint. If I can take all of your data and I can put it on a micro SD, you don't have big data. If I can put all of your data on a micro SD, you do not need to worry about ever deleting any data. Providing your system has been running for more than like a year.
cues.zh: 我知道在座有些人可能在想，但数据随时间肯定会变得非常大。你们有多少人每天处理超过 100 万笔事务？500 万？1000 万。那我给你们个提示。如果我能把你所有数据都放到一张 micro SD 卡上，你就不算有大数据。如果我能把你所有数据都放到一张 micro SD 卡上，你就不必担心删除任何数据——前提是你的系统已经运行了大概一年以上。

cues.en: What you need to consider is where you sit relative to Moore's law. Are you gaining data faster or slower than that exponential curve? And to be fair, I forget the name of the guy. It's another law associated to Moore's law that actually claims data growth is actually faster than Moore's law by a little bit. If you are not going faster than Moore's law, then you don't have to worry about the amount of data that you have. Your data will just continually get cheaper and cheaper and cheaper for you to store.
cues.zh: 你需要考虑的是你相对摩尔定律处在什么位置。你积累数据的速度比那条指数曲线更快还是更慢？说实话，我忘了那个人的名字。有一条与摩尔定律相关的定律，声称数据增长其实比摩尔定律还略快一点。如果你的速度没有超过摩尔定律，那就不必担心你拥有的数据量。你的数据存储只会变得越来越便宜、越来越便宜。

cues.en: If I were to look three years ago, how much would it cost me to get a one terabyte SSD, or one terabyte of SSD? Today, for what, about $500, I can go get a Samsung 840 M-SATA one terabyte SSD drive. Thing will do over 100,000 IOPS. Where do you think we'll be in three years? Where do you think we'll be in five years? So for most of you, do not worry about deleting events. You probably don't need to, and we're gonna talk more about this.
cues.zh: 如果回顾三年前，买一块1TB的SSD要花多少钱？如今，大概500美元就能买到一块三星840 M-SATA 1TB的SSD硬盘。这玩意能跑到10万以上的IOPS。你觉得三年后我们会到什么地步？五年后呢？所以对大多数人来说，不必担心删除事件。你很可能不需要这么做，我们后面会详细讨论。

cues.en: Accountants don't do this. What do accountants do? Accountants, if they transfer 10,000 to your account by accident, and they meant to transfer 1,000, will do one of two things. They will either take 9,000 back, this is known as a partial reversal, and accountants don't like doing this. Okay, sure, if it's 10,000 with 1,000 coming back, it's not too big of a deal, right? What did I intend to do? Yeah, but what was the amount I intended to send then?
cues.zh: 会计可不这么干。会计怎么做呢？会计如果不小心往你账户转了1万，本意是转1千，他们会做两件事之一。要么把9千收回去，这叫部分冲销，会计不喜欢这么干。行吧，如果是一万退回一千，问题不大，对吧？我本来想做什么？对，但我原本打算转的金额是多少？

cues.en: 10,000, 9,000, okay, you guys can figure it out pretty quick. What if there's six accounts involved and they're not perfect even numbers? Now you're gonna be getting out a pencil and a paper and trying to actually work out what was originally intended by me. So accounts don't like doing partial reversals because it's a pain for auditors who are actually reading through the books. They tend to do what's known as a full reversal. And a full reversal, I give you 10,000, I take 10,000 back. And then I say,
cues.zh: 一万、九千，行，你们很快就能算出来。要是涉及六个账户，而且数字还不是整数呢？那你就得拿出纸笔，费力去推算我当初到底想干什么。所以会计不喜欢做部分冲销，因为对真正查账的审计员来说是件麻烦事。他们倾向于做所谓的全额冲销。全额冲销就是，我给你一万，我把一万收回来。然后我说，

cues.en: Here's the 1,000 that I originally intended to do, so now the auditor going through goes, oh, that's a cancellation, and here's what I intended to do. cues.en: object-oriented software construction. I would recommend getting probably version 2 of the second edition. I will warn you, his book seems to be event-sourced. It looks like it's append-only, and he just keeps adding to it on every edition. If you get the third edition, I believe it's 1,300 pages, but on the bright side, you will save money because you don't have to go to the gym. And what CQS states is very simple. There are two types of methods. The first type of method that we have
cues.zh: 面向对象软件构造。我建议你买第二版的第2版。我得提醒你，他的书看起来像是事件溯源式的。它看起来是只追加的，他每一版都在不断往里加内容。如果你买第三版，我相信它有1300页，但往好处想，你能省钱，因为不用去健身房了。而CQS所主张的非常简单。方法有两种类型。我们有的第一种方法

cues.en: has a void return type. It's called a command. If you're in functional code, we could call it a unit return type. It is allowed to mutate state. It is not a pure function. The second type of method that we have has a non-void return type. It is not allowed to mutate state. It is called a query. You'd be amazed if you just follow that in your code how many bugs you'll save yourself from. How many of you run into a problem where you did something like there was something hitting at the top of a loop inside the loop?
cues.zh: 的返回类型是void。它叫命令。如果你在函数式代码里，我们可以叫它unit返回类型。它允许修改状态。它不是纯函数。我们有的第二种方法有非void的返回类型。它不允许修改状态。它叫查询。如果你在代码里遵循这一点，你会惊讶于能避免多少bug。你们有多少人遇到过这样的问题：在循环内部，循环顶部有东西在变化？

cues.en: calling a getter on an object. You said, I know. I'm going to hoist that out of the loop. And in that way, the code will be faster. And then the code stopped working. And you're like, what the hell? I hoisted a getter out of the loop. And then you go look. And the getter was actually a mutating state. And you found a bug. It makes it much, much easier to reason about your code. And the reason that it was so important to do this inside of Eiffel, which is the language that he writes, is because they have something called contracts. And contracts are normally written on top of pure functions.
cues.zh: 在对象上调用 getter。你说，我知道。我要把它提到循环外面。这样代码会更快。然后代码不工作了。你心想，搞什么鬼？我把 getter 提到循环外了。然后你去看。发现这个 getter 其实会修改状态。于是你发现了一个 bug。这会让代码推理变得容易得多。为什么在 Eiffel 里这么做如此重要——Eiffel 是他所写的那种语言——是因为它们有叫契约的东西。而契约通常写在纯函数之上。

cues.en: And what happens if I call your contract twice? Should that somehow alter your behavior? That'd be weird. What if I realize I don't need to call your contract? And now you work differently because I didn't call your contract? That's weird. Now Martin Fowler wrote that CQS is not a principle. It's instead a rather reasonable suggestion. If you know Martin, you can imagine him saying that in his British voice.
cues.zh: 如果我调用你的契约两次会怎样？这应该以某种方式改变你的行为吗？那就怪了。如果我发现我不需要调用你的契约呢？现在你因为我没调用契约就表现不同？这很怪。Martin Fowler 写过，CQS 不是原则。它更像一个相当合理的建议。如果你了解 Martin，你能想象他用英国口音说这句话。

cues.en: And he gives a counter example to CQS. Stack.pop. Does stack.pop return something? Does stack.pop mutate state? Whoops. Now, if I wanted to, I could continue with this. And I could do stack.pop and then stack.value. But that would seem awkward. Have any of you ever looked at how iEnumerable works in .NET? MoveNext in .value? Why not have moveNext return something? It's following CQS.
cues.zh: 他还给了一个 CQS 的反例。Stack.pop。stack.pop 会返回东西吗？stack.pop 会修改状态吗？哎呀。现在，如果我想的话，我可以继续这样。我可以先 stack.pop，再 stack.value。但那会显得别扭。你们有人看过 .NET 里的 IEnumerable 是怎么工作的吗？MoveNext 和 .value？为什么不让 MoveNext 返回点东西？它是在遵循 CQS。

cues.en: And CQRS becomes much more important when we start talking about things in a distributed system. And the reason it becomes so much more important is because we start talking about things like idempotency, where queries are going to be naturally idempotent, commands are not going to be naturally idempotent. CQRS goes one step further than this. And by the way, how many of you have seen something on CQRS that said, underneath it, did you mean cars?
cues.zh: 当我们开始讨论分布式系统中的事务时，CQRS 就变得更加重要了。它之所以变得如此重要，是因为我们开始讨论幂等性这类问题——查询天生就是幂等的，而命令则不是。CQRS 比这更进一步。顺便问一下，你们有多少人看到过关于 CQRS 的内容，下面写着“您是不是要找 cars”？

cues.en: And this is because, back in 2007 or so, if you typed CQRS in Google, it would say, did you mean cars? But now, after years, and I guess enough hits throughout the web, it now actually gives you CQRS links. CQRS just goes one step further than this, and it basically says, we're going to have two objects now. We're going to take one object, which was filled with commands and queries, and we're going to make two objects out of it. One with all the commands, one with all the queries. And actually, they call this a pattern. How weird is that?
cues.zh: 这是因为早在 2007 年左右，如果你在 Google 里输入 CQRS，它会提示“您是不是要找 cars”。但这么多年过去，网上相关内容足够多了，现在它真的会给你 CQRS 的链接了。CQRS 只是比这更进一步，它基本上是说，我们现在要有两个对象了。我们拿一个原本包含命令和查询的对象，把它拆成两个对象。一个放所有命令，一个放所有查询。他们还把这叫做一种模式。是不是挺奇怪的？

cues.en: It's such a simple concept, but it's an enabling pattern. Talk about queries a little bit. When we talk about queries, queries tend to have a different perception of your data, correct? Almost always, a query is focused on a screen and what a screen looks like. Does a screen have anything at all to do with managing your transactional invariance? Probably not.
cues.zh: 这个概念非常简单，但它是一种赋能模式。稍微聊聊查询。当我们谈论查询时，查询对数据的视角往往是不一样的，对吧？几乎总是，查询关注的是某个界面以及界面长什么样。界面跟管理事务不变性有什么关系吗？大概没有。

cues.en: If they do have similarities, it's accidental. There's no causative relationship between this. Screens, or sorry, queries are screen related because you want to do one call across the wire to come back because you'll be perceived as being faster than. Another thing about queries, in most systems, queries are what you need to scale. Most systems I look at,
cues.zh: 就算它们有相似之处，那也是偶然的。这之间没有因果关系。屏幕，或者说查询，是与屏幕相关的，因为你想要一次跨网络调用就能返回结果，这样你会被认为比……更快。关于查询的另一件事是，在大多数系统中，查询是你需要扩展的部分。我看过的大多数系统，

cues.en: Do on the order of one to two orders of magnitude more queries than they do processing of commands. I've seen them all the way up to four or five orders of magnitude. How many of you think that you do one to two orders of magnitude more queries than you do commands? Raise your hands. Okay, now I want to get the set going here. Now see how much intersection we have. How many of you have modeled something around a third normal form database?
cues.zh: 处理的查询量大约比命令处理量多一到两个数量级。我见过高达四到五个数量级的情况。你们中有多少人认为自己处理的查询量比命令量多一到两个数量级？举手。好，现在我想把范围缩小一下。看看有多少重叠。你们中有多少人围绕第三范式数据库建模过？

cues.en: I've actually been brought in by clients where they were having scalability problems. And you found out they were doing 99 queries for every one command. And they had modeled a third normal form database and couldn't figure out why they were having scaling problems. So 99% of your work is reading, so you optimize for rate performance. Cool. Wonder what the problem is here. But queries are generally what we need to scale. And most people, what they're doing today,
cues.zh: 实际上，有客户因为遇到可扩展性问题把我请过去。结果发现他们每条命令对应99个查询。他们用的是第三范式数据库建模，却搞不懂为什么会有扩展性问题。所以你的工作99%是读取，那你就该为读性能做优化。挺好。想知道问题出在哪。但查询通常是我们需要扩展的部分。而大多数人今天所做的，

cues.en: They build up, let's say, a domain model on top of a database. When it comes to scaling, they talk about how to scale everything. We don't need to do that. We can talk about how do we scale our queries and not talk about scaling our commands. There's a really interesting property about queries that makes them especially easy to scale. Commands are hard to scale. Rights are hard to scale. Queries are very easy to scale because almost all queries can operate with relaxed consistency.
cues.zh: 他们在数据库之上构建一个领域模型。谈到扩展时，他们讨论如何扩展所有东西。我们不需要那样做。我们可以讨论如何扩展查询，而不谈扩展命令。查询有一个非常有趣的特性，使它们特别容易扩展。命令难以扩展。写入难以扩展。查询非常容易扩展，因为几乎所有查询都可以在放宽一致性的情况下运行。

cues.en: In other words, queries can be eventually consistent. When it comes time to process a command, I really need my current state in order to be able to do this reliably. It gets very complex if I do it in an eventually consistent way for validation. But queries can almost always be eventually consistent. How many of you make fully consistent queries today? Let's try this another way. How many of you put a pessimistic lock around every query in your system? Guess what? You're already eventually consistent. You just don't know it.
cues.zh: 换句话说，查询可以是最终一致的。到了处理命令的时候，我确实需要当前状态，才能可靠地完成处理。如果用最终一致的方式来做校验，就会变得非常复杂。但查询几乎总是可以做到最终一致。你们中有多少人现在的查询是完全一致的？换个问法。你们中有多少人在系统里给每个查询都加了悲观锁？猜怎么着？你们其实已经是最终一致的了。只是自己不知道。

cues.en: So what happens if I query off to SQL Server? I was asked by the client to make a DTO for them. So I read up the data, I'm building the DTOs, I go to put them into IIS to send it back, and then he goes and changes the data. Do I have a magical yo-yo packet in IIS that will take that HTTP request, route it back to me so I can change it before I send it back to the client? So you are already eventually consistent. You're just not taking advantage of it. We can start taking advantage of it now.
cues.zh: 那么，如果我去 SQL Server 查询会怎样？客户让我给他们做一个 DTO。于是我读取数据，构建 DTO，准备把它们放进 IIS 发回去，结果他这时又去改了数据。难道 IIS 里有个魔法溜溜球数据包，能把这个 HTTP 请求再路由回我这里，让我在发回客户端之前改掉它吗？所以你们已经是最终一致的了。只是没利用这一点。现在我们可以开始利用它了。

cues.en: And queries become super, super easy to scale. And we start looking at a system that looks a bit like this. We're going to have, on one side, which will be the right side. And by the way, I do this talk a lot in Europe, and I always feel bad for the English as a second language people, because the right side is on the left, and very often they get confused. So on one side, we've got our domain objects with application services, normal DDD style stuff.
cues.zh: 而且查询的扩展会变得超级超级容易。我们开始看一个有点像这样的系统。我们会有一侧，也就是右侧。顺便说一句，我在欧洲经常讲这个演讲，我总为英语非母语的人感到难过，因为右边在左边，他们经常被搞糊涂。所以在一侧，我们有领域对象和应用服务，就是正常的 DDD 风格那套东西。

cues.en: And on the other side, we just have this thin read layer that goes directly back to the database, no ORMs or anything crazy like that, and just returns a DTO by querying against the database. This system is very, very easy to scale. How many of these could I make? Could I make 10 of them that are the exact same thing? Put a load balancer in front of 10 databases with 10 thin read layers and 10 remote facades on top of them? So long as your data can fit into one of those databases,
cues.zh: 而在另一边，我们只有一个轻量读取层直接连接数据库，不用 ORM 之类花哨的东西，直接查询数据库返回一个 DTO。这套系统非常、非常容易扩展。这种节点我能做多少个？能做 10 个一模一样的吗？在 10 个数据库前放个负载均衡器，配上 10 个轻量读取层，上面再搭 10 个远程门面？只要单个数据库能装得下你的数据，

cues.en: You are linearly scalable now. You can geographically distribute them. These are all sorts of fun things. And it's almost always queries that are the interesting part with this. To be fair, if anyone here happens to work in finance, yes, I know you get many, many more writes than reads. There are some systems like that, but they're few and far between. Now, OK. Why is that not going to that slide? That's interesting.
cues.zh: 你就能做到线性扩展。你可以做地域分布式部署。玩法多得很。而在这种架构中，真正有意思的几乎总是查询。说句公道话，如果现场有人做金融，是的，我知道你们的写操作远多于读操作。确实有这类系统，但毕竟凤毛麟角。好了，等等，怎么切不过去那页幻灯片？有点意思。

cues.en: Okay, we'll just leave it like this since it doesn't want to go to that slide in full screen mode for some reason. Awesome. I think that was impressed crashing. You gotta love Linux, right? Ah, we can go through these anyway. Because we got these three slides that we can see here and we're gonna go to our summary anyway. Why don't we talk about this as well? Okay. Let's try bringing that one back up. We'll go here. That was lovely.
cues.zh: 好吧，既然全屏模式下不知为何切不过去，我们就先这样吧。太棒了。我觉得是 Impress 崩了。怎么能不爱 Linux 呢？啊，反正我们也能继续讲。因为这里能看到这三张幻灯片，而且我们反正马上也要进总结了。不如顺便把这个也聊聊？好的。试着把它重新调出来。切到这里。真是绝了。

cues.en: Let's see, which one do we have? Not that one. Not that one. OK. Yeah, that one. OK. When we talk about this, it's very uncommon that you will have a single read model. Normally, you will have multiple read models for doing different kinds of queries. And this is what I actually talked about more so last year, which I felt bad, because afterwards, most of the questions I got were more so about basic event sourcing, which is why I am doing a longer talk about basic event sourcing this year.
cues.zh: 看看我们用的是哪个？不是那个。也不是那个。好，就那个。好。说到这个，你很少会只有一个读模型。通常会有多个读模型来处理不同类型的查询。这正是我去年讲得更多的地方，我当时挺不好意思的，因为之后收到的问题大多是关于基础事件溯源的，所以今年我要做一个更长的关于基础事件溯源的演讲。

cues.en: But normally you will use many different types of read models. For instance, I may have a UI that needs to get some data on it. You know what works really well for that? A document database, where the document's basically aligned to what my screens look like. But I may have another thing that wants to do OLAP querying. You know how that crap business people want with reporting and being able to hook up Excel to it? So why not have an OLAP cube for them? And I may want to do full text indexing, so I may use something like Lucene.
cues.zh: 但通常你会使用多种不同类型的读模型。比如，我可能有个 UI 需要获取一些数据。你知道什么最适合这个吗？文档数据库，文档基本上和我的屏幕长得一样。但我可能还有另一个要做 OLAP 查询的东西。你知道那些业务人员想要的那种报表，还能把 Excel 接上去的破事吗？那为什么不给他们弄个 OLAP 立方体呢？我还可能想做全文索引，所以我可能会用 Lucene 之类的东西。

cues.en: But generally, I'm going to have more than one of these. And all of those are just projections. And you can have as many different projections as you want in an event source system. And at any point in time, I can always add a new model, correct? It just starts from event zero and comes forward. Who cares if it takes the weekend? Well, to be fair, you're probably going to make it faster than that if you're doing it often. There's lots of tricks to make these come up faster, like, for instance, switching to batch job versus real time. But could I also, if I started seeing that my OLAP cubes are getting overloaded?
cues.zh: 但一般来说，我会不止有一个这样的东西。而所有这些都只是投影。在事件溯源系统里，你想要多少个不同的投影都行。而且在任何时候，我都可以随时加一个新模型，对吧？它就从事件零开始往前推。谁在乎它是不是要花一个周末？嗯，公平地说，如果你经常做的话，你可能会做得比那更快。有很多技巧可以让这些更快地建起来，比如，切换到批处理作业而不是实时处理。但如果我开始发现我的 OLAP 立方体过载了，我能不能也……

cues.en: I could make three OLAP cubes, correct? And distribute my load between three. This is how people are using these kinds of event source systems. And remember that it's not one read model that you will have. Most systems require two, three, four different read models to actually work well. And there's massive accidental complexity that comes from trying to use only a single read model. Now, to summarize, state transitions are important concepts in our domains.
cues.zh: 我可以建三个 OLAP 立方体，对吧？然后把负载分摊到这三个上。人们就是这样使用这类事件源系统的。记住，你不会只有一个读模型。大多数系统需要两到四个不同的读模型才能真正良好运作。而试图只用一个读模型会带来大量偶然复杂度。总结一下，状态转换是我们领域中的重要概念。

cues.en: The result of an operation, what that means is an important concept. It's a fact. All getters and setters and domain models are code smell. If you start seeing lots of them, start thinking about what you're doing. And the single thing that I want people to walk away from this with is that you cannot, under any circumstances, have a single model that does everything for you and does it well. It doesn't exist. There are different types of models and different models do good at different things.
cues.zh: 操作的结果，它意味着什么，是一个重要概念。它是一个事实。所有的 getter 和 setter 以及领域模型都是代码坏味道。如果你开始看到大量这类东西，就该想想自己在做什么了。我最希望大家带走的一点是：在任何情况下，你都不可能用一个模型包办一切并且做得很好。这种东西不存在。有不同类型的模型，不同的模型擅长不同的事情。

cues.en: And I talked about this last year a lot in polyglot data. But I mean, how many of you have tried using SQL Server full text indexing and compared that to something like Lucene? How many of you have poorly implemented a graph inside of a SQL Server? All of this is accidental complexity. And you will not end up with a single model that will work well for everything. Just like event sourcing doesn't work well for everything. You can't do a query off of your current state in a purely event source system.
cues.zh: 去年我在多语言数据方面谈了很多这个。但我的意思是，你们中有多少人试过用 SQL Server 全文索引，并把它和 Lucene 之类的东西比较过？你们中有多少人曾在 SQL Server 里草草实现过一个图？这些都是偶然复杂度。你最终不会得到一个对一切都好用的单一模型。就像事件溯源也不是对一切都好用。在纯事件源系统里，你无法基于当前状态做查询。

cues.en: You need some piece of transient state to be able to query with it. It will help you and save you a lot of accidental complexity. So with that, I think we have like one minute or one and a half minutes for questions. So if you're persisting your state transition with your events in your event store, is there value in saving your command to correspond with those state transitions? So I tend to save my commands if only so I can see what my external stimuli was.
cues.zh: 你需要某种瞬时状态才能据此进行查询。这会对你很有帮助，免去许多偶然复杂度。讲到这里，我想我们大概还有一到一分半钟的提问时间。提问：如果你在 event store 中通过事件来持久化状态变更，那么保存与这些状态变更对应的 command 是否有价值？我通常倾向于保存命令，哪怕只是为了看清外部的触发诱因是什么。

cues.en: And I use it a lot for looking at how people are using my system. And I use it a lot for things like debugging or smoke testing. But it's not like they're a core part of my system. I do save them, but not everyone does save them. When I load up my aggregate, my aggregate is fully consistent.
cues.zh: 我经常用它来观察人们是如何使用我的系统的。我也经常把它用于调试或冒烟测试这类场景。但它们并不是我系统的核心部分。我确实会保存它们，但并不是每个人都会保存。当我加载我的 aggregate 时，我的 aggregate 是完全一致的。

cues.en: I can tell you the exact number, and it's fully 100% consistent, so I can't avoid that. To be fair, in a warehouse, you're never going to avoid that problem, however, and I'd go back and talk with the business people about this. They want to have a fully consistent warehouse, so how do you stop the people that are stealing and make them check out the inventory appropriately? At the end of the day, the warehouse is the book of record, not the computer system.
cues.zh: 我能告诉你确切的数字，它是 100% 强一致的，所以这点避无可避。平心而论，在实体仓库里你永远避不开那种问题，不过我会回去跟业务方探讨这点。他们想要一个完全一致的仓库，但你怎么阻止有人偷拿、并让他们都老老实实做库存出库呢？归根结底，实体仓库才是最终权威记录，而不是计算机系统。

cues.en: And that kind of stuff does happen. So you will oversell things no matter what. And I would have that conversation with them. But in general, let's imagine that it was something where I really am the book of record. Then when I load up my aggregate for a given inventory item, it is 100% consistent.
